summary: This document defines a URN namespace identifier for generating URNs suitable for use in documentation and in testing or experimenting with URN-related technology.

plainLanguage.summary:
A URN is a name for something that does not say where to fetch it. This RFC sets aside the word 'example' for names that only ever appear in documents and tests, so a sample name can look like a real URN without ever being one.

Anyone can make one up. The name has the form urn:example: followed by a string of ASCII characters the author chooses. Nothing checks it, and these names are never meant to be resolved to anything.

questions: how to write example urns in documentation
what is a urn namespace identifier
subtitle: A reserved 'example' prefix so documents and tests can use URNs that will never collide with real ones.

tldr.problem: Specifications, test suites and manuals need sample identifiers that look real but can never be mistaken for an assigned name.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC registers a formal URN namespace identifier called 'example', so a sample name is written as urn:example: followed by a namespace specific string that the author makes up.
tldr.outcome: Anyone can mint example URNs without registering anything, and they will not collide with current or future real URNs. The names are deliberately not meant to be resolved.

today: RFC 6963 is a Best Current Practice that has not been obsoleted, so the reserved example namespace identifier is still the one to use when writing sample URNs.

sections.title: Why an Example Namespace
sections.content:
The Uniform Resource Name (URN) technology provides a way to generate persistent, location-independent resource identifiers. The scope of a URN comes from its namespace identifier, the short code that appears after urn:. As specified in RFC 3406, there are three kinds of namespace identifier: formal, informal and experimental. Most of the identifiers registered to date are formal.

The experimental kind takes the form X-NID. Because the X- convention has been deprecated in general, this document takes a different route and registers a formal namespace identifier of example, similar to example.com and other reserved domain names.

Under this namespace, specification authors and code developers can mint URNs for documentation, for testing of URN and URI processing, and for URN-related experimentation, by assigning their own unique namespace specific strings, without fear of conflicts with current or future actual URNs.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC sets aside one word, 'example', for names that only appear in documents and tests. A sample name can then look like a real URN without ever being one, and no registration is needed to use it.

sections.title: Requirement Words
sections.content: The document states that the key words MUST, MUST NOT, REQUIRED, SHALL, SHALL NOT, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT, RECOMMENDED, NOT RECOMMENDED, MAY and OPTIONAL are to be interpreted as described in RFC 2119. Those capitalised words set how strongly each rule in the document applies.
sections.plainLanguage: The document uses the standard capitalised words for rules, such as MUST and SHOULD, so a reader can tell which parts are mandatory and which are advice.

sections.title: The Namespace Definition Template
sections.content:
The namespace identifier example is assigned, with registration information of version 1, dated 2013-04-24, and the IETF as the registering organisation, with the IESG as designated contact.

The declared syntactic structure is urn:example:{NSS}. The namespace specific string, abbreviated NSS, is a mandatory string of ASCII characters that conforms to the URN syntax requirements and provides a name that is useful within the relevant documentation example, test suite or other application.

The template settles the remaining questions. Those who mint example URNs ought to strive for uniqueness in the NSS, but such uniqueness cannot be guaranteed through the assignment process, so it is NOT RECOMMENDED to use example URNs for any purpose other than documentation, private testing and truly experimental contexts. Once minted, an example URN is immutable, although the document or test suite that uses it need not be. Assignment is completely open, since anyone can mint example URNs. Example URNs are not intended to be resolved, and the namespace will probably never be registered with a Resolution Discovery System, except to inform requesters that the URNs are merely examples. The rules for lexical equivalence specified in RFC 2141 apply, there is no validation mechanism, and the scope of an example URN is limited to the documentation, test or experiment in which it is found.
sections.plainLanguage: The name always has the same shape: urn:example: followed by a string the author invents. You are asked to make that string unique, but nothing checks it, so these names stay inside the document or test that uses them and are never resolved.

sections.title: Why a Formal Namespace Was Needed
sections.content:
No existing formal namespace enables entities to generate URNs that are appropriate for use as examples in documentation and in URN-related testing and experimentation. It could be argued that no such formal namespace is needed, given that experimental namespaces can be minted at will. However, experimental namespaces run afoul of the trend away from using the X- convention in the names of protocol parameters and identifiers.

In practice, specification authors often mint examples using fake namespace identifiers that go unregistered because they were never intended to be used. To minimise the possibility of confusion, use of this dedicated example namespace is recommended for generating example URNs.
sections.plainLanguage: Authors used to write fake namespace codes such as X-whatever, but that convention has been retired. Giving one reserved word to examples removes the guesswork and keeps sample names from being mistaken for real ones.

sections.title: How Example URNs Are Minted
sections.content:
The example namespace identifier is intended to provide a clean, easily recognisable space for minting examples to be used in documentation and in URN-related testing and experimentation. The NSS is best as a unique string, generated by the person, organisation or other entity that creates the documentation, test suite or other application. There is no issuing authority for example URNs, and it is not intended that they can be resolved in any meaningful way.

The namespace does not remove the need to coordinate with issuing authorities for existing namespaces. Minting urn:example:xmpp:foo instead of requesting issuance of urn:xmpp:foo is still the right move, new namespace identifiers must still be registered when existing namespaces do not match the desired functionality, and the basic spirit of namespace identifier assignment still applies, such as setting up shadow identifiers like urn:example:MyCompany:* instead of using HTTP URIs.
sections.plainLanguage: You make up the rest of the name yourself; no authority issues it. But a real namespace identifier is still needed for anything that must work in production, so example names stay for examples.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document introduces no additional security considerations beyond those associated with the use and resolution of URNs in general.
sections.plainLanguage: The document adds no security rules of its own. The usual care around URNs applies.

sections.title: The IANA Registration
sections.content: The document defines a URN namespace identifier registration of example, which IANA has added to the Formal URN Namespaces registry. The completed registration template can be found in Section 3 of the document.
sections.plainLanguage: The word 'example' is now on IANA's list of formal URN namespaces, so any tool can recognise it.
